entities.name: Forza Italia
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Forza Italia ('Let's Go Italy'), founded in 1994 by media magnate Silvio Berlusconi in 90 days using his Mediaset television empire's organizational infrastructure, transformed Italian politics by becoming the first major party in European democracy created primarily through television advertising and celebrity founder charisma — without a traditional party organization, trade union base, or ideological tradition. Berlusconi governed Italy as prime minister three times (1994-1995, 2001-2006, 2008-2011) — more than any post-war Italian leader — combining unprecedented conflicts of interest between government authority and media ownership.

Berlusconi created Forza Italia after the 1993-1994 Tangentopoli ('Bribesville') corruption scandal destroyed Italy's traditional party system (Christian Democracy, Socialist Party, Communist Party). His three commercial television channels (Canale 5, Italia 1, Rete 4) had created a mass audience culture that he converted directly into a voter base through saturation advertising. The party was named after a football chant, and club memberships were organized through Mediaset corporate structures.

Berlusconi's three governments were characterized by attempts to change laws that applied to his own legal cases (including trials for bribery, tax fraud, and underage prostitution), and the most extreme conflict of interest in any European democracy — a prime minister who controlled 90% of Italian TV broadcasting. His 2011 resignation during the European debt crisis, while crowds celebrated in the streets of Rome, marked the end of his governing career. Berlusconi's death in June 2023 was followed by Forza Italia's continuation under Antonio Tajani as a moderate conservative coalition partner.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Forza Italia was the first major European party created through television advertising and celebrity founder charisma — pioneering the media-party model that influenced Trump, Macron, and every subsequent personality-driven political movement, while demonstrating the corruption risks of media-government conflict of interest.
